Admin / privileged API call without a preceding SUCCESSFUL login (JWT forgery indicator) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Forged tokens signed with the hardcoded 'random' secret never traverse the application's login or refresh flows — they appear as bearer-auth-only requests. This UC pivots web access logs for /api/v1/admin/* and /api/v1/me hits whose source IP has no /api/v1/login/* 2xx in the prior 24h, the behavioural signature of token forgery. Rationale: The advisory's PoC explicitly hits /api/v1/admin/users, /api/v1/me, and /api/v1/token/refresh with a forged Bearer token (no login step). Modelling 'admin hit without a recent successful login from same IP' captures that footprint without requiring the JWT to be parsed. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Long-lived legitimate session whose original login was >24h ago (refresh token kept it alive)
  • Service-to-service auth using a static API key rather than the login flow
  • Healthcheck / synthetic monitoring hitting /api/v1/me with a pre-baked token
  • CI smoke tests that obtain tokens out of band and never use /login
  • NAT'd corporate egress where many users share one source IP and not all have logged in
Suppression filter
and csUserName !in ("healthcheck","synthetics","datadog","newrelic") and csUserAgent !has_any ("Pingdom","StatusCake","Datadog Synthetics","kube-probe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the JWT from the Authorization header — decode header+payload (no signature check needed) and verify the 'sub' and 'roles' claims match a real user. Compare 'iat' against the user's last legitimate login from your IdP. 2) Contain: if the token is forged, rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET to a 32+ byte random value, restart the Go service, and force-revoke all sessions. Block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pull all requests from the same IP and from the same user-agent over the prior 30 days. Look for /api/v1/admin/users enumeration, mass /api/v1/me lookups across different sub claims (token re-use across identities), and any state-changing POST/PUT/DELETE that may have already exfiltrated data.
let AdminHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(24h)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("/api/v1/admin/","/api/v1/me","/api/v1/token/refresh")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl;
let LoginHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(48h)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("/api/v1/login/","/api/v1/auth/")
    | summarize LastLogin = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP;
AdminHits
| join kind=leftouter LoginHits on RemoteIP
| where isnull(LastLogin) or datetime_diff('hour', Timestamp, LastLogin) > 24
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LastLogin, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let AdminHits = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/api/v1/(admin/|me$|token/refresh)"
    | where scStatus < 400
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csUriStem, csUserAgent, csUserName;
let LoginHits = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(48h)
    | where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/api/v1/(login|auth)"
    | where scStatus < 400
    | summarize LastLogin = max(TimeGenerated) by cIP;
AdminHits

| where isnull(LastLogin) or datetime_diff('hour', TimeGenerated, LastLogin) > 24
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csUriStem, csUserAgent, csUserName, LastLogin
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internal host clones / curls github.com/dhax/go-base or raw dev.env AIReconnaissance Medium
Catches developer or attacker hosts pulling the vulnerable boilerplate — either via 'git clone github.com/dhax/go-base', 'go get', or direct curl/wget of raw.githubusercontent.com/dhax/go-base/.../dev.env. Either action seeds the secret 'random' onto a system that may later run the service or be used to forge tokens. Rationale: Hits the exact module path github.com/dhax/go-base from the advisory's Affected Component plus the raw.githubusercontent.com pattern used when an attacker just wants the leaked dev.env without cloning. Narrowing to git/go/curl/wget keeps the volume sane. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base
ATT&CKT1593.003 T1588.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer learning Go and trying the popular boilerplate (1,685 stars on GitHub)
  • Security researcher pulling the repo to reproduce the CVE
  • CI mirror sync that mirrors many public Go modules including go-base
  • Internal training material that references go-base as an example
  • Dependency-resolution side-effect when a transitive module points back here
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("renovate","dependabot","snyk.exe","trivy.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate the host — is it a dev workstation, a build agent, or a production server? Production server is the worst case. Capture the destination path of the clone to know where the secret 'random' now lives on disk. 2) Contain: if production, rip out the deployed artifact and rebuild from a patched commit (>= cc82b9740fa6). On dev hosts, ensure the dev.env file is not later copied into a release container. 3) Hunt: from the same host/user, look for subsequent 'go build' artifacts being pushed to internal registries, container image pushes labelled with the developer's name, and any web service deployed from those artifacts now serving /api/v1/* on the network.

JWT token in HTTP Authorization header verifying against secret 'random' AIActions on Objectives High
Decodes Bearer JWTs from web access logs and verifies their HMAC-SHA256 signature against the literal key 'random'. A successful verification is a smoking-gun forged token from the public CVE-2026-48031 secret. This is the highest-confidence detection but requires a custom enrichment step in the SIEM ingestion pipeline. Rationale: Implements the article's exact PoC inversely — the attacker uses 'random' as the HMAC key to sign; we use it to verify. Any token that verifies with key='random' is, by definition, a forged token because patched versions log.Fatal on that secret. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base/pull/31
ATT&CKT1606.001 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentester actively exploiting the CVE during an authorised engagement
  • Pre-prod environment that still ships the unpatched dev.env intentionally for testing
  • Bug-bounty researcher submitting a PoC against the production endpoint
  • An unrelated service that coincidentally also uses HS256 with the (weak) key 'random' for a different purpose
  • Token-replay testing tools (e.g. Burp JWT extension) being run by red team
Suppression filter
and SourceIP !in (KnownPenTesterIPs) and not (Environment == "staging" and ServiceName startswith "goose-base-test-")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the affected endpoint is running github.com/dhax/go-base. Decode the JWT 'sub' and 'roles' claims and check whether they correspond to a real user or a fabricated identity. Any 'roles' containing 'admin' is automatic priority-1. 2) Contain: rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET to `openssl rand -base64 32`, redeploy the service to invalidate all outstanding tokens, force-logout all users, then patch the dhax/go-base dependency past commit cc82b9740fa6. Block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pull every request from the offending IP over 30d; cross-correlate with DB audit logs for /api/v1/admin/users access, profile reads (/api/v1/me), and any state-mutating POST/PUT/DELETE. Identify what was touched and prepare a breach-notification scope.
// Requires custom Authorization-header capture into AdditionalFields on DeviceNetworkEvents.
// Decoded JWT verification is performed at ingest; this query surfaces records flagged JWTForged=true.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| extend Forged = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).JWTForgedWithKnownWeakSecret)
| where Forged == "true"
| extend JWTSubject = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).JWTSubject)
| extend JWTRoles = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).JWTRoles)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, JWTSubject, JWTRoles, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Requires a Logstash / Logic App enrichment that decodes Bearer JWTs and stamps a custom field 'JWTForgedWithKnownWeakSecret'=true when HMAC-SHA256 verifies against 'random'.
let Forged = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

    | where Forged == "true"
    | extend JWTSubject = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalExtensions).JWTSubject)
    | extend JWTRoles = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalExtensions).JWTRoles)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceName, SourceIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, JWTSubject, JWTRoles, RequestClientApplication;
Forged
| order by TimeGenerated desc
@jwt.forged_with_known_weak_secret:true OR @jwt.signing_key:random
# log group: /aws/applicationelb/access-logs  (ALB access logs — adjust per ELB; requires custom Lambda enricher that stamps jwt_forged=true)

Compromised Rust crate onering performs code exfiltration

Aikido
2026-06-10 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The compromised onering Rust crate v1.4.1 on crates.io shipped a malicious build.rs that exfiltrates the diff of your latest commit to a hosted Sentry endpoint every time you build. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1195.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Cargo dependency manifest or download pinned to compromised onering 1.4.1
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network egress to onering Sentry exfil ingest domain or project envelope path · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cargo build script spawning git with onering's exfil --pretty=format JSON · [LLM] build.rs invoking curl POST to Sentry envelope endpoint with code diff payload · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Cargo build script spawning git with onering's exfil --pretty=format JSON AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the onering 1.4.1 build.rs harvesting host repo metadata by spawning `git log -n 1 --pretty=format:{"commit":"%H","author":"%an",...}` from a Cargo build-script process. The JSON pretty-format template plus a Cargo build-script parent is the article-specific fingerprint of the exfil step. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim --pretty=format JSON template strings the article shows in the build.rs payload (`commit`, `%H`, `author`, `%an`, `email`, `%ae`) combined with a Cargo build-script parent (rustc compiles build.rs to a binary named `build-script-build` on Windows/Linux). Routine `git log` calls from IDEs/CI don't carry this exact JSON tag set parented by a build-script process. Cross-checked the build-script-build naming via the official Cargo build-script reference (doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html) and the upstream maintainer issue https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1 • https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html
ATT&CKT1005 T1195.001 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer tooling (rust-analyzer, IDE git extensions) running git log with --pretty=format but using a CSV/tab template, not the JSON tag set above
  • CI scripts running git log --pretty=format from a shell, not parented by build-script-build
  • Custom internal Rust crates whose legitimate build.rs invokes git for version-stamping (usually only `git rev-parse HEAD`, not multi-field JSON metadata)
  • Cargo workspace tooling like `cargo-edit` or `cargo-release` shelling out to git from rustc context
  • Manual test of the cenotelie/onering repository itself by a researcher reproducing the IOC
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "rev-parse" and not (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("%H", "%an", "%ae")))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture full process tree (cargo→rustc→build-script-build→git), the Cargo.lock and Cargo.toml on the host, and the user's home repo path; confirm `onering` 1.4.1 is in the dependency graph (`cargo tree | grep onering`). 2) Contain: isolate the dev workstation from the network, kill the cargo build, revoke any source-control PATs the user has cached (gh, git credential-manager), and force-push-protect any branches the user touched in the last 24h. 3) Hunt: query DeviceNetworkEvents for the same DeviceId reaching o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io or any /api/4511539669368912/envelope/ POST in the last 30 days, pivot on every other host that resolved that domain, and search Cargo.lock files repo-wide for `onering` at v1.4.1.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("git.exe", "git")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "log"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--pretty=format"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("commit", "%H", "author", "%an", "email", "%ae")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("build-script-build.exe", "build_script_build.exe", "build-script-build", "cargo.exe", "rustc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\git.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/git"
| where CommandLine has "--pretty=format"
| where CommandLine has_all ("commit", "%H", "author", "%an")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("build-script-build", "build_script_build", "cargo.exe", "rustc.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

build.rs invoking curl POST to Sentry envelope endpoint with code diff payload AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the onering build.rs exfiltration POST: curl invoked with the specific Sentry envelope URL (project id 4511539669368912 / org id o4511539639222272) and the `application/x-sentry-envelope` Content-Type, parented by a Cargo build-script process. This is the network-layer half of the exfil chain. Rationale: Article gives the verbatim Sentry ingest URL, DSN public key, organization id and project id. Curl parented by a Cargo build-script with any of those four strings in the cmdline is essentially deterministic for the onering payload. The combination forecloses noise from legit Sentry users (none would have curl invoked by build-script-build) and from legit Cargo builds (none would POST to a Sentry envelope). Cross-checked the Sentry envelope endpoint format at docs.sentry.io/api/envelopes/. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.sentry.io/api/envelopes/ • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1
ATT&CKT1041 T1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Project legitimately using Sentry crash-reporting from Rust code, but invoked via the sentry-rust SDK at runtime (not via curl in a build script)
  • Developer manually testing the IOC for IR/research purposes from the same host
  • Internal Sentry-on-prem mirror where the URL happens to contain the same project id substring
  • Penetration-test simulation of supply-chain exfil using these exact IOCs
  • Threat-intel platform crawler fetching the article URL into a curl trace logged by EDR
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the curl process tree, extract the POST body if proxy/PCAP available, and confirm the DSN public key 8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821 in the URL path. Pull Cargo.lock on the host and grep for `onering`. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the cargo build, block o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io at the proxy, rotate any source-tree secrets the recent commit may have touched (treat the recent diff as exposed). 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the destination domain across the fleet for the last 30 days; pivot on every internal repo whose Cargo.lock contains onering 1.4.1; alert affected dev leads that recent commits leaked.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe", "curl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io", "4511539669368912/envelope", "application/x-sentry-envelope", "8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("build-script-build.exe", "build_script_build.exe", "build-script-build", "cargo.exe", "rustc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/curl"
| where CommandLine has_any ("o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io", "4511539669368912/envelope", "application/x-sentry-envelope", "8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("build-script-build", "build_script_build", "cargo.exe", "rustc.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network egress to onering Sentry exfil ingest domain or project envelope path AICommand & Control High
Wire-side catch-all for hosts reaching the article's Sentry ingest domain or the project-specific `/api/4511539669368912/envelope/` path — independent of the process that initiated it (covers proxied/wrapped variants and Linux/macOS dev hosts where Cargo runs). Rationale: Article names the exact ingest hostname `o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io` and project envelope path `/api/4511539669368912/envelope/`. Domain alone is so specific that any internal DNS resolution or HTTP request to it is high-confidence — and catches process variants (the maintainer's GitHub repo is also compromised, so the payload could land via `git clone` rather than crates.io). 30-day lookback because exfil-per-commit means even one historical hit is interesting. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Project legitimately using a Sentry org with the same numeric org-id (collisions are astronomically unlikely for this specific id but technically possible)
  • Threat-intel platform proxy fetching the article or IOC bundles citing the domain
  • Detection-engineering lab host reproducing the IOC for rule tuning
  • Internal Sentry-on-prem instance whose path namespace happens to coincide (won't share the public DNS name)
  • Browser preview from analyst clicking the article URL
Response runbook
1) Triage: enrich the source host with cargo / Rust toolchain inventory and recent process tree; identify the process that owned the egress (curl vs sentry-rust SDK vs something else). 2) Contain: sinkhole `o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io` at corporate DNS and add a deny on the URL path at the egress proxy; isolate impacted hosts; treat the most recent git diff on each impacted repo as leaked and rotate any secrets it touched. 3) Hunt: dump every host that resolved the domain in the last 90 days; for each, run `cargo tree` against every repo on disk for `onering` 1.4.1; check the maintainer's GitHub repo (https://github.com/cenotelie/onering) is pinned to a vetted commit, not main.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io" or RemoteUrl has "4511539669368912/envelope"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort),
(DeviceEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
 | where AdditionalFields has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImWebSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Url has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io" or Url has "4511539669368912/envelope"
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr),
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DnsQuery has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName),

 | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestMethod)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cargo dependency manifest or download pinned to compromised onering 1.4.1 AIDelivery Medium
Catches the supply-chain ingress: file writes to Cargo.lock / Cargo.toml mentioning the malicious crate version, or HTTPS downloads of the onering 1.4.1 crate tarball from crates.io. Targets the build-time moment when a dev pulls the poisoned dependency, before build.rs runs. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit IOC `onering 1.4.1 from crates.io`. Cargo writes the cache file `onering-1.4.1.crate` under `~/.cargo/registry/cache/<index>/` and updates Cargo.lock with the pinned version on resolve — both are deterministic side-effects of pulling the poisoned dep. Article also flags that the GitHub repo is compromised, so we keep the file-write detection generic enough to fire on git-cloned dependencies (where the URL fetch wouldn't trigger). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1 • https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registries.html
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or detection engineer intentionally fetching the IOC for sandboxing
  • Mirror/proxy of crates.io pre-fetching the malicious version into local cache before a yank propagates
  • Vulnerability scanner like cargo-audit or Aikido enumerating the version
  • Legacy CI pipeline still referencing onering 1.4.1 after yank but on an isolated build agent
  • Developer cleaning up `Cargo.lock` after a known-bad pull (Cargo writes the file even on `cargo update --precise` to a safe version, with onering removed)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the host's `~/.cargo/registry/cache/**/onering-1.4.1.crate` and confirm SHA256 matches the malicious tarball; grep every repo on disk for `onering` in Cargo.lock and note the version. 2) Contain: instruct the dev to `cargo update -p onering --precise <safe-version>` or remove the dependency, force a fresh `cargo build` in a clean target dir, and on shared CI invalidate the cargo cache. 3) Hunt: across the org's source-control, run `git grep -E 'onering.*=.*"1\.4\.1"'` on every Rust repo; check internal Cargo mirrors for any hosts that pulled the bad version; coordinate with Aikido feed for org-wide blast radius.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has "crates.io" and (RemoteUrl has "onering/1.4.1" or RemoteUrl has "onering-1.4.1.crate")
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl),
(DeviceFileEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where FileName in~ ("Cargo.lock", "Cargo.toml")
 | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cargo.exe", "cargo")
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where FolderPath has ".cargo\\registry\\cache" or FolderPath has ".cargo/registry/cache"
 | where FileName has "onering-1.4.1"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImWebSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Url has "crates.io" and (Url has "onering/1.4.1" or Url has "onering-1.4.1.crate")
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod),
(ImFileEvent
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where TargetFileName in~ ("Cargo.lock", "Cargo.toml")
 | where ActingProcessName has "cargo"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine),
(ImFileEvent
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where TargetFileName has "onering-1.4.1"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

(#event_simpleName=FileWritten (TargetFileName=/onering-1\.4\.1/i OR (TargetFileName=/[\\/](Cargo\.lock|Cargo\.toml)$/i ContextImageFileName=/cargo(\.exe)?$/i))) OR (#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(static\.)?crates\.io/i)

Use Defender TVM software vulnerability data — these CVEs are all in the June 2026 KB rollup and require none of the others to be exploitable. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE list pulled out of the article body (CVE-2026-45657/47291/44815/45585/45655/45658/50507/45586/49160 plus the two non-Microsoft CVE-2025-10263 and CVE-2026-8863). TVM joins keep it to vulnerable software actually installed, not just the CVE catalogue.

Step 3: Hunt — pivot on the still-exposed devices into the other UCs in this set (HTTP.sys/DHCP child-process anomalies, MaxHeadersCount registry tampering, CTFMON LPE) to confirm none have already been exploited pre-patch.

HTTP/2 Bomb mitigation tampering — MaxHeadersCount registry value (CVE-2026-49160) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Watch for write, delete, or downward modification of the new `MaxHeadersCount` registry value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\HTTP\Parameters. Microsoft introduced this value specifically to mitigate the HTTP/2 Bomb DoS against IIS/HTTP.sys (CVE-2026-49160). An attacker who reaches admin on an IIS host could remove or set it to 0 to re-enable the DoS surface; conversely the value going from set→unset on a host that previously had it is a tampering signal. Rationale: Pulls the exact registry path and value name (`MaxHeadersCount` under `HTTP\Parameters`) that the article quotes Microsoft as introducing in the June 2026 update. Tamper-with-the-mitigation is a higher-fidelity signal than trying to detect the HTTP/2 Bomb payload itself on the wire, which IIS logs don't expose at header-count granularity.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually applying or tuning the new mitigation (legitimate IIS hardening sweep)
  • Configuration management tools (DSC / Ansible / GPO) deploying the registry value across an IIS fleet
  • Microsoft KB rollback during a problematic patch cycle
  • IIS performance team raising the limit above default for a high-header app
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","MsiExec.exe","services.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — pull `InitiatingProcessFileName` and account; legitimate sets come from `services.exe`/`TrustedInstaller.exe` or known CM agents. Anything signed by an interactive user, cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or LOLBins is suspicious. Step 2: Contain — if change is unexpected, restore the value (>= 100 is Microsoft's default, see KB) and snapshot the IIS host. Step 3: Hunt — look back 24h on the same host for w3wp.exe spawning shells, IIS module installs (`appcmd.exe install module`), or unexpected HTTP/2 traffic spikes; pivot to the HTTP.sys/IIS anomalous-child UC.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\HTTP\Parameters"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "MaxHeadersCount"
| where ActionType in~ ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueDeleted","RegistryKeyDeleted")
| extend NewVal = tostring(RegistryValueData), PrevVal = tostring(PreviousRegistryValueData)
| where ActionType != "RegistryValueSet" or NewVal in ("0","0x0","") or toint(NewVal) < toint(coalesce(PrevVal,"0"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, NewVal, PrevVal,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\HTTP\Parameters"
| where RegistryValue =~ "MaxHeadersCount"
| where EventType in~ ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueDeleted","RegistryKeyDeleted")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData,
          RegistryPreviousValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DHCP Client svchost anomalous child process (CVE-2026-44815 post-exploit) AIExploitation High
CVE-2026-44815 is a pre-auth stack-overflow RCE in the Windows DHCP Client. The DHCP Client service runs in svchost.exe under the `LocalServiceNetworkRestricted` host with the `Dhcp` service argument. Successful exploitation would surface as svchost (DHCP-hosted) spawning a non-svchost child — there is essentially no legitimate reason for `Dhcp`-hosted svchost to create a shell, script host, or LOLBin. Rationale: Article: 'CVE-2026-44815 ... allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network ... systems handling DHCP traffic should be treated as high-priority patch targets.' DHCP Client svchost normally never spawns shells; pairing the parent (`-s Dhcp` / `LocalServiceNetworkRestricted`) with the LocalService SID and a LOLBin child is a low-FP combination.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft DHCP troubleshooting kits running `ipconfig.exe` under the service context
  • Endpoint management agents (Intune/SCCM) invoking `net.exe` via the DHCP host briefly during network re-init
  • MDM remediation scripts that target DHCP renewal
  • Sysinternals procdump / handle.exe by IR team taking dumps of svchost
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has "ipconfig /renew"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — confirm the parent command line really contains `-s Dhcp` (not another svchost service); pull the SHA256 of the child and the network connections from the same `InitiatingProcessId` ±5 min. Step 2: Contain — isolate the host with Defender 'Isolate device' or NAC quarantine; capture the DHCP packet trace if still online (rogue DHCP server may be persistent on the LAN). Step 3: Hunt — across the same subnet, look for additional DHCP Client hosts that received a DHCP OFFER from the same MAC, and pivot to the patch-inventory UC for CVE-2026-44815 to find other still-vulnerable hosts on the same broadcast domain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-s Dhcp", "-s dhcp", "LocalServiceNetworkRestricted")

HTTP.sys / IIS w3wp.exe spawning shell or LOLBin (CVE-2026-47291 post-exploit) AIExploitation High
CVE-2026-47291 is an integer overflow in HTTP.sys (kernel) allowing unauthenticated network RCE. Post-exploitation in IIS environments typically surfaces as the w3wp.exe app-pool worker spawning cmd/powershell or LOLBins, or as `System` process anomalies. This rule pivots on the w3wp parent → suspicious child shape which is essentially absent in healthy IIS operations. Rationale: Article: 'CVE-2026-47291 ... integer overflow ... in Windows HTTP.sys that allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.' HTTP.sys is a kernel driver, but IIS deployments funnel HTTP.sys traffic into w3wp.exe app-pool workers — successful exploitation gives the attacker code in that context. w3wp spawning cmd/PowerShell is high-fidelity (legitimate web apps rarely shell out).
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy ASP.NET apps using `Process.Start("cmd /c ...")` for legitimate batch work (e.g. PDF rendering, ImageMagick wrappers)
  • SharePoint or Exchange Health Manager scripts that invoke PowerShell from w3wp
  • WebDeploy / msdeploy.exe operations during application deploys
  • Web-based admin consoles (HelpDesk apps, ITSM portals) that legitimately invoke `net.exe`/`whoami.exe` on behalf of authenticated admins
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !contains "WebDeploy" and ChildCmd !contains "msdeploy"
| where ParentCmd !contains "HealthMailbox"
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — pull the parent w3wp.exe command line to identify the IIS App Pool (`-ap` argument). Check if that pool is on a known-legacy/known-shells allowlist for the org; if not, treat as live. Step 2: Contain — recycle the App Pool, capture a memory dump of w3wp.exe via Sysinternals procdump, and isolate the host. Pull the IIS access logs for the 5 minutes prior — large or malformed POSTs to .aspx/.asmx handlers are the likely vector. Step 3: Hunt — search the IIS inetpub wwwroot folders for new .aspx/.ashx/.config files created by the IIS worker (web shells), and pivot to CVE-2026-47291 patch status across the IIS fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe","ipconfig.exe","hostname.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain,
          ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentIntegrity=InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel,
          ChildImage=FolderPath,
          ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildIntegrity=ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| extend NewBase = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where NewBase in ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe","ipconfig.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TargetUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CTFMON spawning elevated child or CTFMON-hosted privilege escalation (CVE-2026-45586 / GreenPlasma) AIExploitation Medium
CVE-2026-45586 is a privilege-escalation flaw in the Windows Collaborative Translation Framework (CTFMON), publicly disclosed as a zero-day and suspected to be the GreenPlasma PoC released by Chaotic Eclipse. CTFMON normally only spawns IME/language helpers at the user's own integrity level. Detection: ctfmon.exe (or its CTF API consumers) spawning a child at High/System integrity, or an integrity-level escalation event whose initiating process is ctfmon.exe. Rationale: Article: 'CVE-2026-45586 ... Windows Collaborative Translation Framework (CTFMON) privilege escalation' and 'suspected to be a fix for a zero-day privilege escalation exploit that Chaotic Eclipse released under the name GreenPlasma.' ctfmon.exe legitimately spawns only language-bar helpers at the user's own integrity. A high-integrity child from a medium-integrity parent is a textbook LPE signal.
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows Error Reporting auto-launching wermgr.exe/WerFault.exe under ctfmon — filtered above
  • MUI / language pack installer running under TrustedInstaller (parent would already be High integrity — caught by the integrity-delta filter)
  • Sysinternals AccessChk by an IR team checking CTF token integrity
  • RDP language input service restart during a console handoff
Suppression filter
| where ChildImage !has @"\Windows\WinSxS\"
| where ParentImage !has @"\Windows\WinSxS\"
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — confirm the integrity delta (parent Medium / child High or System). Pull the SHA256 of the spawned child binary and any registry writes by ctfmon ±60s (CTFMON COM hijack patterns write to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\CTF). Step 2: Contain — kill the elevated child, isolate the host, capture a memory dump of ctfmon.exe and the elevated child. Step 3: Hunt — back-search 30 days for the same SHA256 anywhere in the fleet (likely PoC artefact named after GreenPlasma/MiniPlasma), and pivot to the CVE-2026-45586 patch-status UC to find unpatched hosts that could be next.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "ctfmon.exe"
| where FileName !in~ ("ctfmon.exe","conhost.exe","wermgr.exe","WerFault.exe")
| where ProcessIntegrityLevel in~ ("High","System")
| where InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel !in~ ("High","System")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain,
          ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentIntegrity=InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel,
          ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage=FolderPath,
          ChildIntegrity=ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\ctfmon.exe"
| extend NewBase = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where NewBase !in ("ctfmon.exe","conhost.exe","wermgr.exe","werfault.exe")
| where TokenElevationType in ("%%1936","%%1937")  // Full Token (admin) — the LPE outcome
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TargetUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: CTFMON Spawning Elevated Child (CVE-2026-45586 GreenPlasma LPE)
id: 7a1e4c83-6f2b-4a93-b5c1-d4e8f1a02c3d
description: Detects ctfmon.exe (Collaborative Translation Framework) spawning a child process at High or System integrity from a non-elevated parent context. Consistent with exploitation of CVE-2026-45586 — the CTFMON privilege-escalation zero-day publicly disclosed by Chaotic Eclipse as 'GreenPlasma' before the June 2026 patch.
references:

author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/12
tags:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:(*\\ctfmon.exe OR *\\Ctfmon.exe OR *\\CTFMON.EXE)) (@IntegrityLevel:(High OR System)) -@Image:(*\\ctfmon.exe OR *\\Ctfmon.exe OR *\\conhost.exe OR *\\WerFault.exe OR *\\wermgr.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/ctfmon\.exe$/i

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentImageFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, UserName, IntegrityLevel], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmd values(Processes.process_integrity_level) as child_integrity values(Processes.parent_process_integrity_level) as parent_integrity from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="ctfmon.exe" Processes.process_integrity_level IN ("high","system") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where parent_integrity!="high" AND parent_integrity!="system"

PoC artefact drop — Chaotic Eclipse named exploits (YellowKey, GreenPlasma, MiniPlasma, RoguePlanet, bitskrieg) AIInstallation Low
Article references five publicly-released PoCs by researcher Chaotic Eclipse (aka Nightmare-Eclipse): YellowKey (CVE-2026-45585 BitLocker bypass), GreenPlasma (CVE-2026-45586 CTFMON LPE), MiniPlasma (CVE-2020-17103 print spooler incomplete fix), RoguePlanet (Microsoft Defender race-condition to SYSTEM cmd), and bitskrieg (CVE-2026-50507 BitLocker full-data bypass). Hunt for file writes or process executions whose name or folder contains these PoC code-names — researchers and red-teamers commonly preserve the published name in repo/binary names, and uplifted commodity attackers often do not bother to rename. Rationale: Article explicitly names the five Chaotic Eclipse / Nightmare-Eclipse PoCs (YellowKey for CVE-2026-45585, GreenPlasma for CVE-2026-45586, MiniPlasma against CVE-2020-17103, RoguePlanet for the Defender race condition, bitskrieg for CVE-2026-50507). String-name hunting is low-precision but high-recall; useful for catching unsophisticated reuse of the public PoCs before defenders patch.
ATT&CKT1588.005 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red team / pentest engagement legitimately downloading the PoCs to a test host
  • Security researchers in the org investigating the PoCs in a sandbox VM
  • Threat intel team archiving copies for analysis
  • Documentation / blog posts (.html, .pdf) referencing the names — high FP on browser cache hits
  • Wallpaper or theme files coincidentally named (yellow key, etc.)
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\Default\Cache\"
| where FolderPath !has @"\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Cache\"
| where FileName !endswith ".pdf" and FileName !endswith ".html" and FileName !endswith ".htm"
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — distinguish PoC binaries (.exe, .ps1, .py, .dll) from documentation files (.pdf, .html, .docx). For binary hits, pull SHA256 and check it against VirusTotal / internal sandbox. For doc hits, check user role (red team / IR / researcher allowlist). Step 2: Contain — if a binary executed on a non-research host, isolate and capture memory + the binary. Confirm whether the corresponding CVE patch was applied; if not, the host may already be compromised at the privilege level the PoC achieves (SYSTEM for RoguePlanet/GreenPlasma, encrypted-data access for YellowKey/bitskrieg). Step 3: Hunt — pull the InitiatingProcessAccountName and look 24h back/forward for that user's other activity (downloads, browser, USB). Pivot to the patch-status UC for the matching CVE.
let Codenames = dynamic(["yellowkey","greenplasma","miniplasma","rogueplanet","bitskrieg"]);
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
    | extend low_name = tolower(FileName), low_path = tolower(FolderPath)
    | where low_name has_any (Codenames) or low_path has_any (Codenames)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | extend low_cmd = tolower(ProcessCommandLine), low_img = tolower(FolderPath), low_name = tolower(FileName)
    | where low_name has_any (Codenames) or low_img has_any (Codenames) or low_cmd has_any (Codenames)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
union FileHits, ProcHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let Codenames = dynamic(["yellowkey","greenplasma","miniplasma","rogueplanet","bitskrieg"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| extend low_path = tolower(TargetFilePath), low_name = tolower(TargetFileName)
| where low_name has_any (Codenames) or low_path has_any (Codenames)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium

ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",

    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.initial-access
logsource:

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

phpBB instance vulnerable to CVE-2026-29199 (3.3.16 and below / 4.0.0-a2) exposed on managed assets AIReconnaissance High
Surface owned web hosts running phpBB at or below 3.3.16, or 4.0.0-a2 — the versions Aikido confirmed are exploitable by a single unauthenticated HTTP request that yields a valid session as any user, including administrators. Asset-side hunt is the first step before pivoting to exploit-pattern detection; the article explicitly withheld payload details to give admins time to upgrade. Rationale: Aikido article explicitly names vulnerable versions (3.3.16 and below, 4.0.0-a2) and CVE-2026-29199. Cross-checked phpBB 3.3.17 release notes (phpbb.com viewtopic 2672170), SentinelOne CVE database entry, and Infosecurity-Magazine coverage. TVM is the cleanest pivot since Aikido deliberately withheld exploit payload until the patch window closes. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty — vulnerability-management data is not in the listed Datadog standard sources, not an FDR event_simpleName, and not a CloudTrail/VPC/GuardDuty signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29199/ • https://www.phpbb.com/community/viewtopic.php?t=2672170 • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/phpbb-authentication-bypass/ • https://www.phpbb.com/support/documents.php?mode=changelog&version=3

phpBB password-reset Host header injection (CVE-2026-29199 exploitation) AIExploitation High
POST to phpBB's password-reset endpoint `ucp.php?mode=sendpassword` where the HTTP Host header on the request does NOT match the site's canonical hostname allow-list. This is the request shape that lets an unauthenticated attacker poison the reset email — phpBB derives the reset link from the inbound Host header when `force_server_vars` is unset, so the victim follows a link to attacker.tld and the single-use token is delivered to the attacker. Rationale: Article describes a single-HTTP-request unauth account takeover; SentinelOne's CVE-2026-29199 write-up specifies the root cause as Host-header trust in `ucp.php?mode=sendpassword` when `force_server_vars` is disabled, and phpBB 3.3.17 release notes (phpbb.com 2672170) confirm the fix. The detection anchors on the article-specific endpoint + the corroborated trust-boundary violation. Defender XDR has no native web-access-log table so defender_kql is left empty. Datadog has no standard web-access-log source in the listed schema (nginx/apache custom integrations would need a pipeline) — left empty rather than fabricated. Falcon FDR does not ship web server access logs as an event_simpleName — empty. CloudWatch path empty unless AWS WAF logs are present (not in the listed canonical log groups). Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29199/ • https://www.phpbb.com/community/viewtopic.php?t=2672170 • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/phpbb-authentication-bypass/
ATT&CKT1190 T1566.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate phpBB instance reachable via multiple aliased hostnames not yet added to the canonical allow-list
  • Reverse proxy / CDN (Cloudflare, Akamai) inserting an X-Forwarded-Host but the origin Host header points at the internal origin name
  • Vulnerability scanner (Qualys, Tenable, Acunetix) probing the password-reset endpoint with a synthetic Host header
  • User-misconfigured custom domain on a hosted phpBB that hasn't propagated to ops' canonical list
  • phpBB instance bound to a raw IPv4 address — Host header is the IP, not a name
Response runbook
1. Triage: extract the anomalous Host value and the requesting SrcIpAddr; check if the value is a known typosquat (paypa1.com style) or a recently-registered domain, and whether the source IP recently hit the same `sendpassword` endpoint with the legit Host (recon-then-exploit shape). 2. Contain: temporarily WAF-block POSTs to `ucp.php?mode=sendpassword` with any Host other than the canonical allow-list; force-revoke any password-reset tokens issued in the last 24h via phpBB ACP; if internet-facing, set `force_server_vars=true` with explicit `server_name`/`server_protocol` in `config.php` immediately. 3. Hunt: pull outbound mail logs from the phpBB server for password-reset emails sent in the last 7d and check whether the Reset URL contains a non-canonical hostname; pivot to victim mailboxes for the same window to see if any user clicked an inbound reset link they didn't initiate.
let CanonicalHosts = dynamic(["forum.example.com","www.example.com"]);   // REPLACE with your phpBB canonical hostnames
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "ucp.php" and Url has "mode=sendpassword"
| where isnotempty(HttpHostName)
| extend HostLower = tolower(HttpHostName)
| where not(HostLower in~ (CanonicalHosts))
| where not(HostLower matches regex @"^(\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}$")   // ignore direct-IP probes if you want raw signal — remove this line to keep them
| summarize Count=count(), DistinctSrc=dcount(SrcIpAddr), SampleSrc=make_set(SrcIpAddr,5), SampleUA=any(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent), SampleReferer=any(HttpRequestHeaderReferer) by DstHostname, HostLower, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

phpBB OAuth account-binding CSRF — anomalous traffic to pre-3.3.17 OAuth callback path AIExploitation Medium
Hunt for the pre-patch OAuth callback path (`ucp.php` with `oauth_service=` / `mode=login_link` / `login=external`) being hit with cross-site referrers or unusual session-cookie state — the request shape that exploits the CSRF + state-validation flaw allowing an attacker to silently bind their own OAuth credential to a victim's logged-in phpBB session (one of the two improper checks disclosed in 3.3.17 release notes; no click required on one variant). Post-patch this path is replaced by `/user/oauth/authenticate/...` so legitimate traffic should be migrating away. Rationale: phpBB 3.3.17 release notes (phpbb.com 2672170) describe two improper OAuth checks — one a CSRF + state-validation bypass that needs only a logged-in victim to load a crafted URL — and explicitly state the redirect URI handler has moved to `/user/oauth/authenticate/...` (the only code block in the original Aikido article). Inferring the pre-3.3.17 callback shape from phpBB convention (ucp.php with oauth_service / mode=login_link / login=external query params) is the closest article-grounded pivot until the second Aikido post drops technical details. Marked hunting + Medium confidence because legitimate OAuth flows look very similar — operators must tune CanonicalHosts. Defender empty (no native web log table); Datadog empty (no standard web log source in schema); Falcon empty (web access logs not in FDR event_simpleName set); CloudWatch empty (not a CloudTrail/VPC/GuardDuty signal). Cross-checked against: • https://www.phpbb.com/community/viewtopic.php?t=2672170 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29199/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/phpbb-authentication-bypass/
ATT&CKT1098 T1550.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Google/Facebook/GitHub OAuth provider redirecting to a phpBB instance whose admin hasn't yet updated the redirect URI to /user/oauth/authenticate/... — the Referer will look 'external' (accounts.google.com / facebook.com) for genuine logins
  • User clicks a forum-share link from an external blog/social site that lands on a phpBB page mid-OAuth flow
  • Internal-monitoring or uptime checker hitting the OAuth callback as part of a synthetic transaction
  • phpBB cross-instance content embeds — referrer is another forum the user was browsing
  • Security scanner (Aikido Attack, Acunetix, Burp) probing the legacy OAuth endpoint as part of a CVE-2026-29199 verification
Response runbook
1. Triage: for each hit, check whether the destination phpBB instance is still pre-3.3.17 (TVM/UC1 hit) — post-patch this endpoint should be dead and any traffic is either misconfig or probing. Confirm the Referer host is not an expected OAuth provider domain (accounts.google.com, github.com, login.facebook.com). 2. Contain: rotate the phpBB site's OAuth provider client secrets in case the bind succeeded; in phpBB ACP review `phpbb_user_group` for accounts whose `group_id` changed in the last 14 days, and review the `oauth_accounts` table for new bindings without a corresponding user-initiated link event in the application audit log. 3. Hunt: pivot to UC2 on the same dest host and timeframe for prior recon, and to UrlClickEvents / EmailEvents for inbound `ucp.php?oauth_service=` links sent to staff mailboxes (the no-click variant still needs the URL delivered somehow — phishing email, forum DM, watering-hole).
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let CanonicalHosts = dynamic(["forum.example.com","www.example.com"]);   // REPLACE with your phpBB canonical hostnames
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where Url has "ucp.php"
| where (Url has "oauth_service=") or (Url has "mode=login_link" and Url has "login=external")
| extend Referer = tolower(coalesce(HttpRequestHeaderReferer,""))
| extend RefererHost = extract(@"^https?://([^/]+)", 1, Referer)
| extend IsExternalReferer = iff(isempty(Referer), true, not(RefererHost in~ (CanonicalHosts)))
| where IsExternalReferer == true
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestHeaderReferer, HttpRequestHeaderCookie
| summarize Count=count(), DistinctSrc=dcount(SrcIpAddr), Sources=make_set(SrcIpAddr, 8), Referers=make_set(HttpRequestHeaderReferer, 4), SampleUrl=any(Url), SampleUA=any(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent) by DstHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Defender RoguePlanet Zero-Day Grants SYSTEM Access on Updated Windows

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The anonymous security researcher going by the name Chaotic Eclipse (aka Nightmare-Eclipse) has released a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for yet another Microsoft Defender zero-day named RoguePlanet. "The exploit is a race condition, so it's a hit or miss," the researcher, who published the exploit under a new GitHub account "MSNightmare" said. "I have managed to get a 100% success rate on

CVEsCVE-2026-33825 CVE-2026-45498 CVE-2026-41091
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1204.004 T1528
Domainsprojectnightcrawler.dev
