File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108") or SHA1 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108") or MD5 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108") or SHA1 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108") or MD5 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WinRAR Flaw Exploited by Russia-Aligned Groups to Deploy Stealers in Ukraine

The Hacker News
2026-06-09 16 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Two Russia-aligned cyber attack campaigns have continued to exploit a security flaw in WinRAR to target Ukrainian organisations, almost a year after patches for the vulnerability were released. The activity has been attributed by Trend Micro to Earth Dahu (aka Gamaredon) and SHADOW-EARTH-066 (aka UAC-0226). It involves the exploitation of CVE-2025-8088, a path traversal flaw that allows an

WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 — archive tool writes payload to user Startup folder AIInstallation High
Detects the smoking-gun signature of CVE-2025-8088 NTFS ADS path traversal: WinRAR/Rar/UnRAR/7zG writing files into %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup — the exact persistence drop chain used by SHADOW-EARTH-066 (GIFTEDCROOK) and Earth Dahu (GammaPhish/GammaLoad) campaigns against Ukrainian organisations. Rationale: Article explicitly states the CVE-2025-8088 exploit chain drops an LNK 'placed in the Startup folder so that it's automatically executed every time a user logs in' — combining archive-tool parent with Startup-folder destination + autostart extension is article-specific and behaviourally near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against Trend Micro disclosure and ESET's earlier RomCom write-up of the same CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-8088 • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/romcom-exploits-winrar-zero-day-cve-2025-8088/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0047/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1574.005 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT-deployed software bundles where WinRAR/7-Zip is used in scripted installers that legitimately drop launcher shortcuts into the Startup folder
  • User extracts a legitimate portable app archive and manually pins an LNK into Startup (rare but seen on dev/power-user workstations)
  • Backup-restore operations where an old user profile is recovered with Startup-folder content via WinRAR
  • Software-deployment tools (PDQ Deploy, SCCM staging) chain-calling WinRAR/UnRAR to expand a vendor MSI bundle
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PDQDeploy","sccm","sccmclient","InstallShield","setup.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the dropped artefact (LNK/EXE/DLL), SHA256 it, and check VT + the article's known-bad hashes; inspect the parent RAR file in DownloadedFiles / mail attachments. 2) Contain — isolate the host via MDE Live Response, kill any running powershell/cmd/mshta children spawned in the next 5 minutes, and quarantine the dropped Startup artefact. 3) Hunt — sweep the org for the parent RAR hash, any sibling NTFS:$DATA ADS writes by the same WinRAR process tree, and pivot on the user mailbox for the inbound phishing message that delivered the archive (last 14 days).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("WinRAR.exe","Rar.exe","UnRAR.exe","7zG.exe","Bandizip.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
| where FileName endswith ".lnk" or FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".bat" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".hta" or FileName endswith ".cmd" or FileName endswith ".ps1"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe","7zg.exe","bandizip.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("lnk","exe","dll","bat","vbs","hta","cmd","ps1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:

  - attack.t1059.003

Startup LNK spawns cmd.exe → PowerShell in-memory DLL loader (GIFTEDCROOK chain) AIInstallation High
Catches the GIFTEDCROOK post-extraction loader chain: explorer.exe auto-runs a Startup LNK that invokes cmd.exe which spawns powershell.exe carrying in-memory reflective-load primitives to launch result.dll. Article calls out cmd→PowerShell→reflective-load as the exact sequence. Rationale: Article describes the chain verbatim: 'LNK in Startup folder ... spawns a PowerShell loader via cmd.exe, which then uses in-memory DLL loading to ultimately launch ... result.dll.' Triple-anchor (Startup-LNK parent + cmd→PS + reflective-load tokens) is highly article-specific and rare in benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620/ • https://www.cert.gov.ua/article/giftedcrook
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1620 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate sysadmin login script that uses cmd.exe → powershell.exe -EncodedCommand from an admin's pinned Startup shortcut
  • Citrix/RDS broker scripts triggered from per-user logon LNKs (some EHRs/VDI gold images still ship these)
  • Vendor monitoring/inventory tools that use cmd→PS reflective load (LANDesk, older Tanium build-out scripts)
  • Developer-machine PowerShell profile that imports modules via Reflection.Assembly from a Startup shim
Suppression filter
| where not (ActorUsername has_any ("admin","svc-") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Import-Module","-File \\\\","\\Scripts\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — capture the powershell.exe command line + decode any base64; if it references result.dll or in-memory load, treat as confirmed GIFTEDCROOK loader and pull the Startup LNK + its $DATA streams. 2) Contain — isolate host, kill the powershell.exe tree, quarantine the LNK target and any DLLs written by the PS session in the prior 60 seconds. 3) Hunt — query DeviceNetworkEvents from the powershell.exe ProcessId for callbacks to the article's IPs/domains; sweep all hosts for the same LNK target hash and same parent RAR.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Startup\", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup", ".lnk")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("FromBase64String","IEX","Invoke-Expression","DownloadString","Reflection.Assembly","[Reflection.Assembly]","::Load(","-nop","-w hidden","-windowstyle hidden","-enc","result.dll")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "cmd.exe"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Startup\", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup", ".lnk")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("FromBase64String","IEX","Invoke-Expression","DownloadString","Reflection.Assembly","::Load(","-nop","hidden","-enc","result.dll")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE) @ParentCommandLine:(*"\\Startup\\"* OR *"\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup"* OR *.lnk*) @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\pwsh.exe) @CommandLine:(*FromBase64String* OR *Reflection.Assembly* OR *::Load(* OR *IEX* OR *Invoke-Expression* OR *-nop* OR *hidden* OR *-enc* OR *result.dll*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/cmd\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| ParentCommandLine=/(\\Startup\\|\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup|\.lnk)/i
| regex("(FromBase64String|Reflection\\.Assembly|::Load\\(|IEX|Invoke-Expression|-nop|hidden|-enc|result\\.dll)", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="cmd.exe" AND (Processes.parent_process="*\\Startup\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup*" OR Processes.parent_process="*.lnk*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND (Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*Reflection.Assembly*" OR Processes.process="*::Load(*" OR Processes.process="*IEX*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*" OR Processes.process="*hidden*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*") by host Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
GIFTEDCROOK browser credential and cookie theft — non-browser process reads Chromium/Firefox stores AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects GIFTEDCROOK's credential-collection stage: a process that is NOT the browser itself opens the Login Data, Cookies, Web Data or Firefox key4.db/logins.json/cookies.sqlite files inside the user's browser profile directories. Article names Chrome, Edge, Opera and Firefox as the targets. Rationale: Article enumerates exact targets: 'passwords and cookies from Chromium-based browsers (Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and Opera) and Mozilla Firefox.' File-access pattern from non-browser process is the highest-signal credential-theft pivot available without YARA. Matches GIFTEDCROOK behavior in Trend Micro and CERT-UA reports. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/giftedcrook • https://blog.sekoia.io/gamaredon-toolset/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Credential-manager browser plugins backed by a helper EXE (1Password Helper, Bitwarden-cli)
  • Endpoint backup agents (Code42/CrashPlan, Druva) that snapshot the entire user profile including the browser data directory
  • DLP agents (Forcepoint, Netskope) that scan profile contents on first sync
  • User-account migration tools (USMT, Microsoft Edge Profile Importer, Chrome migration helper) during machine provisioning
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("1Password.exe","1PasswordHelper.exe","Bitwarden.exe","keeperpasswordmanager.exe","code42service.exe","crashplanservice.exe","druvainsync.exe","nsdiag.exe","fcdblog.exe","USMT.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm the reading process is not on the allow-list; SHA256 the binary, check parent process tree back to explorer.exe/cmd.exe/PowerShell to determine entry vector. 2) Contain — isolate host, force-reset all stored credentials and active SSO sessions for the affected user (Entra revoke + browser-side sign-out), rotate any saved API keys, kill the offending process. 3) Hunt — pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 across the fleet; check DeviceNetworkEvents from the same ProcessId for exfil to article IOCs; review EmailEvents for the inbound RAR.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Opera Software\Opera Stable\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","places.sqlite")
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","opera.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","backgroundTaskHost.exe"))
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Opera Software\Opera Stable\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","places.sqlite")
| where not(ActingProcessName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","opera.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","backgroundTaskHost.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GIFTEDCROOK / Gamaredon C2 callback to article IOCs (IPs + workers.dev / trycloudflare / .ru domains) AICommand & Control Medium
Network-level pivot on the article's published infrastructure: three IPs and seven domains spanning Cloudflare Workers, trycloudflare quick tunnels and Russia-tied vanity domains used by SHADOW-EARTH-066 and Earth Dahu after pivoting away from Telegram as their exfil channel. Rationale: All ten IOCs are taken directly from the article's provided IOC bundle (3 IPs, 7 domains) and triangulate two distinct campaigns sharing the CVE. The workers.dev + trycloudflare-quick-tunnel + .ru-vanity-domain combination is the article-specific tradecraft signature post-Telegram-blocking pivot. Triple-pivot (DNS, network, proxy) maximises catch rate. Cross-checked against: • https://otx.alienvault.com/indicator/domain/dayobtvoyu.ru • https://www.virustotal.com/gui/ip-address/172.86.76.132 • https://blog.sekoia.io/gamaredon-toolset/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate dev/test traffic to other tenants on the workers.dev or trycloudflare.com shared CDN — possible but the specific subdomains are unique
  • Sandbox/research VM in the same network deliberately detonating GIFTEDCROOK samples
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment agent that performs active checks against the same IOCs
  • Security researcher browsing the article and clicking links to defanged-but-still-resolvable IOCs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("CuckooMon.exe","vmtoolsd.exe","sandbox-agent.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX-","DETONATE-","MALLAB-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — identify the InitiatingProcessFileName that made the call; if it's powershell/wscript/mshta/cmd/rundll32, treat as confirmed C2. 2) Contain — block the IPs at the firewall/secure-web-gateway, sinkhole the domains in internal DNS, isolate any host that connected in the last 30 days. 3) Hunt — for every host that touched any IOC pull the parent RAR file, LNK Startup artefact, and any FileWritten events under the user's AppData in the 24h before contact; check EmailEvents for the inbound message that delivered the archive.

Earth Dahu / Gamaredon HTA-to-VBScript chain (mshta.exe spawning wscript/cscript) AIDelivery High
Detects Earth Dahu's documented HTA-to-VBScript delivery chain: mshta.exe loading GammaPhish HTA, then spawning wscript.exe/cscript.exe to execute GammaLoad VBScript downloaders that pull GammaSteel. Article confirms this chain has been active since September 2025 and through at least April 2026. Rationale: Article quotes Trend Micro: 'Earth Dahu used the vulnerability with an HTA-to-VBScript infection chain that delivered espionage modules' — mshta.exe → wscript.exe parent-child with a remote/.hta argument is the canonical GammaPhish→GammaLoad pivot. Cross-checked with Sekoia's recent Gamaredon write-up and MITRE G0047. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/gamaredon-toolset/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0047/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/005/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1059.005 T1105 T1568.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business application that ships .hta installers (rare but seen in healthcare and Ukrainian government estates)
  • Sysadmin running diagnostic .hta scripts from Microsoft KB downloads
  • Vendor support tools (Dell SupportAssist older builds, some HP printer setup utilities) launched via mshta.exe
  • Internal IT job that wraps a vbscript downloader for software inventory
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("HELPDESK-","SCCM-") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\\\corp.local\\","\\\\fileserver\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — extract the .hta URL/path from ParentCommandLine, fetch it in a sandbox, hash the dropped VBScript and compare against the article's published hashes (GammaLoad/GammaSteel families). 2) Contain — isolate the host, kill the mshta/wscript tree, block the .hta URL at the proxy, sinkhole any Dead-Drop-Resolver-style domain returned in the GammaLoad fetch chain. 3) Hunt — sweep DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound calls from wscript/cscript to non-Microsoft hosts in the last 30 days; pull EmailEvents and DeviceFileEvents from WinRAR for the inbound RAR that triggered the chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".hta","http://","https://","javascript:","vbscript:")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any (".vbs",".vbe",".js",".jse","GetObject(","WScript.Shell","MSXML2.XMLHTTP","WinHttp.WinHttpRequest")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "mshta.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (".hta","http://","https://","javascript:","vbscript:")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".vbs",".vbe",".js",".jse","GetObject(","WScript.Shell","MSXML2.XMLHTTP","WinHttp.WinHttpRequest")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-43284", "CVE-2026-43500", "CVE-2024-21182", "CVE-2026-0257", "CVE-2026-45659")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-43284", "CVE-2026-43500", "CVE-2024-21182", "CVE-2026-0257", "CVE-2026-45659")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-43284", "CVE-2026-43500", "CVE-2024-21182", "CVE-2026-0257", "CVE-2026-45659")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

New FROST Attack Lets Websites Track What Sites and Apps You Open via SSD Timing

The Hacker News
2026-06-09 7 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious website can work out which sites you visit and which apps you open, using nothing but JavaScript and the timing of your SSD. The attack, called FROST, needs no native code, no extension, and no permission prompt. You open the page, leave the tab sitting there, and it watches the drive for contention in the background. Researchers at Graz University of Technology built it and

Browser writing oversized OPFS file (potential FROST SSD-timing side-channel) AIReconnaissance Low
Hunts for a browser process (Chrome/Edge/Firefox/Safari) writing a file >4 GB into the per-origin Origin Private File System storage path. FROST requires an OPFS file larger than physical RAM so reads bypass the page cache and reach the SSD — legitimate OPFS use rarely exceeds a few hundred MB, so an unexplained multi-GB OPFS allocation is the only host-side tell the Graz paper offers. Rationale: Anchored on the only host-side artefact the article actually names: 'watching your browser's storage for an unexplained multi-gigabyte file is another tell.' The >4 GB threshold mirrors FROST's stated requirement (file > physical RAM to defeat the page cache). Browser-process scope + per-origin OPFS path roots (Chrome/Edge: 'File System/' inside the profile; Firefox: 'storage/default/...fs/'; Safari/WebKit: 'Library/Safari/Storage' or 'Library/WebKit') are taken from the standardised OPFS-on-disk locations referenced by the W3C spec the article cites. No external corroboration searched — there is no actor / malware family / CVE attached, and the IOCs extracted by the pipeline (malicious.app, victim.com, receiver.app, sender.app) are clearly academic placeholders from the paper, not real C2.
ATT&CKT1592.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • In-browser IDEs (StackBlitz WebContainers, VS Code for the Web, Replit, GitPod) which legitimately allocate multi-GB OPFS sandboxes for projects
  • Web-based media editors (Photopea, Figma, CapCut Web) caching large source files
  • Browser-based games persisting asset bundles or save state to OPFS
  • Profile sync / migration tooling temporarily staging the user's browser profile inside the same directory tree
  • Service-worker caches for offline-first PWAs (e.g. mapping apps) that legitimately swell over time
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("stackblitz", "webcontainer", "vscode-web", "replit", "gitpod", "photopea", "figma", "capcut"))
// Add per-tenant: exclude origin folders for sanctioned in-browser IDEs / editors after one pass of investigation
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the origin that owns the OPFS slice (the path component immediately under '/File System/' or '/storage/default/' is the URL-encoded origin). Check the user's recent browser history / open tabs for that origin and whether it is a known-good web IDE / media editor. Pull the parent browser commandline to confirm it's an interactive session and not a headless automation harness. Step 2 — Contain: if the origin is unknown / suspicious, ask the user to close the tab (article notes the measurement only runs while the tab is open) and clear site-data for that origin in browser settings. Snapshot the OPFS file before deletion for forensic review. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same origin across the fleet — if multiple users have a >4 GB OPFS slice from the same domain, that domain is the indicator, not the file size. Also review whether the same browser session enabled cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP headers) by checking proxy/Zscaler/CSP-report telemetry, since FROST

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","Google Chrome","firefox","Safari","com.apple.WebKit.Networking")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\File System\", "/File System/", "/storage/default/", ".mozilla/firefox", "/Library/Safari/Storage", "/Library/WebKit")
| where FileSize > 4000000000  // 4 GB — FROST requires file > physical RAM
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize,

title: Browser writes oversized Origin Private File System (OPFS) file - possible FROST SSD timing side-channel
id: 3f1e9a2c-1d6e-4f0a-9c4f-2b9b5e6a7c01
status: experimental
description: Detects a browser process allocating an unusually large file (>4 GB) inside its per-origin OPFS storage directory. The FROST attack (Graz Univ. of Technology, DIMVA 2026) requires an OPFS file larger than physical RAM so SSD-timing reads bypass the page cache.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-frost-attack-lets-websites-track.html
author: detection-engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:
  - attack.t1592.004
  - attack.reconnaissance
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '/Google Chrome'
      - '/firefox'
      - '/Safari'
      - '/com.apple.WebKit.Networking'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\File System\'
      - '/File System/'
      - '/storage/default/'
      - '.mozilla/firefox'
      - '/Library/Safari/Storage'
      - '/Library/WebKit'
  selection_size:
    FileSize|gte: 4000000000
  condition: all of selection_*
falsepositives:
  - In-browser IDEs (StackBlitz WebContainers, VS Code Web, Replit, GitPod local) genuinely use multi-GB OPFS
  - Web-based video / photo editors caching large media (Photopea, Figma, CapCut Web)
  - Browser-based game engines persisting save state / asset bundles
level: low
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) @EventID:11 (@Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe) OR @process.name:(chrome OR firefox OR Safari OR Google\ Chrome)) (@TargetFilename:(*\File\ System\* OR */File\ System/* OR */storage/default/* OR *.mozilla/firefox/* OR */Library/Safari/Storage/* OR */Library/WebKit/*)) @file.size:>4000000000
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|Safari|WebKit)/i
| regex("(File System|storage/default|\\.mozilla/firefox|Library/Safari/Storage|Library/WebKit)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=[sum(WrittenBytes, as=BytesWritten), min(@timestamp, as=FirstSeen), max(@timestamp, as=LastSeen)])
| BytesWritten > 4000000000

| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, max(Filesystem.file_size) as max_size from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","Google Chrome","firefox","Safari","com.apple.WebKit.Networking") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\File System\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/File System/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/storage/default/*/fs/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.mozilla/firefox/*/storage/default/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/Library/Safari/Storage/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/Library/WebKit/*/Storage/*") AND Filesystem.file_size>4000000000 by host, user, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, max(Filesystem.file_size) as max_size from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","Google Chrome","firefox","Safari","com.apple.WebKit.Networking") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\File System\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/File System/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/storage/default/*/fs/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.mozilla/firefox/*/storage/default/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/Library/Safari/Storage/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/Library/WebKit/*/Storage/*") AND Filesystem.file_size>4000000000 by host, user, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

Hades PyPI Attack: 19 Packages Poisoned to Auto-Run Bun Credential Stealer

The Hacker News
2026-06-09 15 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The Miasma supply chain campaign has sparked a fresh attack wave called Hades, this time involving 37 malicious wheel artifacts across 19 packages in the Python Package Index (PyPI) registry, as the Mini Shai-Hulud-style attacks continue to be refined and splintered to target specific ecosystems. "The compromised releases shipped a *-setup.pth file that attempts to execute automatically

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Hades/Miasma PyPI poisoned package installation (26 named packages) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hades PyPI Attack: 19 Packages Poisoned to Auto-Run Bun Credential Stealer
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Python interpreter downloading Bun runtime ZIP from oven-sh GitHub release · [LLM] Hades persistence: *-setup.pth file written into Python site-packages · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Hades C2: GitHub commit search for campaign markers TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime / firedalazer
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Bun runtime reading developer credential files (.npmrc / .pypirc / .ssh / .env / cloud configs) · [LLM] gh-token-monitor service install or rm -rf wiper command (Hades self-destruct) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Hades/Miasma PyPI poisoned package installation (26 named packages) AIDelivery High
Detects pip / python invoking installation of any of the 26 PyPI packages and versions Socket / StepSecurity identified in the Hades wave of the Miasma supply-chain campaign. Catches the very first foothold before the *-setup.pth hook runs on next interpreter start. Rationale: Uses the verbatim 26 package names from the article's two Hades clusters (the 19-package PyPI cluster + the 7-package bioinformatics cluster). Pip-install command line with these exact names is effectively zero-FP outside of incident-response activity.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DFIR / threat-intel analyst intentionally pulling the package into a sandbox for reverse engineering
  • Internal package-mirror sync (e.g. Artifactory / Nexus PyPI proxy) caching the malicious release before takedown
  • Bioinformatics researcher pulling a legitimately-named-but-coincidental fork via an internal index URL
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !contains "sandbox" and FolderPath !has "\\malware_analysis\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot to DeviceFileEvents on the same host for any *-setup.pth file created after the install and any DeviceNetworkEvents to github.com/oven-sh/bun within 30 min — confirms full chain executed. 2) Contain: isolate host, revoke all developer secrets present (GitHub PAT, npm/PyPI tokens, AWS/GCP/Azure keys, .ssh/*, Anthropic/Claude/MCP configs), force-rotate before reconnecting. 3) Hunt: search the org for any other host that pulled the same package versions in the last 14 days; check internal package mirrors for cached copies; check GitHub org for any repo with description matching 'Hades*The End for the Damned' indicating exfil happened.
let HadesPkgs = dynamic(["bramin","cmd2func","coolbox","dynamo-release","executor-engine","executor-http","funcdesc","magique","magique-ai","mrbios","napari-ufish","nucbox","okite","pantheon-agents","pantheon-toolsets","spateo-release","synago","ufish","uprobe","embiggen","ensmallen","gpsea","mflux-streamlit","nhmpy","ppkt2synergy","pyphetools"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","pip","pip3","python.exe","python","python3","python3.exe")
      or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","pip","pip3","python.exe","python","python3","python3.exe"))
| where ProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (HadesPkgs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let HadesPkgs = dynamic(["bramin","cmd2func","coolbox","dynamo-release","executor-engine","executor-http","funcdesc","magique","magique-ai","mrbios","napari-ufish","nucbox","okite","pantheon-agents","pantheon-toolsets","spateo-release","synago","ufish","uprobe","embiggen","ensmallen","gpsea","mflux-streamlit","nhmpy","ppkt2synergy","pyphetools"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip","python") or ParentProcessName has_any ("pip","python")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (HadesPkgs)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python interpreter downloading Bun runtime ZIP from oven-sh GitHub release AIInstallation High
Hades/Miasma stages a JavaScript stealer by having the malicious .pth or __init__.py hook download the standalone Bun runtime ZIP from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases. Detecting Python/pip as the parent of that network connection is the cleanest cross-platform pivot — Bun is not a Python dependency in any normal supply chain. Rationale: Article: 'The compromised releases shipped a *-setup.pth file that attempts to execute automatically during Python startup, download the Bun JavaScript runtime, and run an obfuscated JavaScript payload named _index.js.' StepSecurity also notes Bun is downloaded as a standalone ZIP — pivoting on python→github.com/oven-sh/bun is the staging-link signature.
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually running 'pip install bun-py' or any pip wrapper that legitimately fetches Bun for a project
  • CI job using a Python-based installer/bootstrap (e.g. Ansible play that installs Bun on a dev workstation)
  • Container build step where a Python entrypoint legitimately bootstraps a Bun-based JS toolchain
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun-py","install-bun","@nestjs","bunx"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent python's command line — was the install one of the 26 Hades package names? Pull DeviceFileEvents for any .pth or _index.js write between the Python start and the Bun download. 2) Contain: kill the Bun process tree, isolate host, snapshot ~/.bun and any extracted ZIP for forensics, revoke every dev secret the user owns (GitHub PAT, npm token, PyPI token, AWS/GCP/Azure CLI creds, Anthropic/Claude API key). 3) Hunt: look across the org for any other host where python.exe was the parent of a github.com/oven-sh/bun fetch in the last 30 days; check GitHub Actions audit log for the user's PAT scopes being used from unfamiliar runners.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pip.exe","pip3.exe","bash","sh","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com/oven-sh/bun","objects.githubusercontent.com")
   and (RemoteUrl has_any ("bun-linux","bun-windows","bun-darwin","/releases/download/") or RemoteUrl endswith ".zip")
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pip.exe","pip3.exe")
       or FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pip.exe","pip3.exe")
    | project DeviceId, PyTimestamp = Timestamp, PyCmd = ProcessCommandLine
) on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (PyTimestamp .. PyTimestamp + 10m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, PyCmd
| order by Timestamp desc
let BunUrlFrag = dynamic(["github.com/oven-sh/bun","objects.githubusercontent.com"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any (BunUrlFrag)
| where Url has_any ("bun-linux","bun-windows","bun-darwin","/releases/download/") or Url endswith ".zip"
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","pip")
    | project DvcHostname, PyTime = TimeGenerated, PyCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine
) on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (PyTime .. PyTime + 10m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, PyCmd
| order by TimeGenerated desc
